title: ETFs and Mutual Funds
summary: SAME BASKET → DIFFERENT MECHANICS → DIFFERENT FEE
subtitle: Two ways to buy a thousand companies at once. They solve the same problem. They just work differently underneath.

blocks.text: Buying single stocks one at a time is slow, costly and risky. It puts all your eggs in a handful of baskets.
Funds solve that. Instead of picking single companies, you buy one product that holds hundreds or thousands of them at once.

There are two main ways to do this in Canada: mutual funds and ETFs. They solve the same problem but work differently underneath, and the Investment Fees lesson showed that the biggest difference is often cost.
Own a slice of the whole market without paying for more than you need.
blocks.detail: Knowing how funds are bought, priced and managed helps you choose one that fits your goals and your budget.
blocks.extra: Section 05 introduces the simplest option for most beginners.

sections.title: What they actually have in common

blocks.text: Mutual funds and ETFs both pool money from many investors into one fund. Both hold a mix of investments: stocks, bonds or both. Both let you own a small slice of a large, spread-out basket without buying each piece.
The difference isn’t what they hold. It’s how you buy them, how they’re priced and, usually, how they’re managed.

How you buy them. A mutual fund is usually bought through a bank or an adviser. An ETF trades on a stock exchange, like a single stock. You buy it through a brokerage account, any time the market is open.

How they’re priced. A mutual fund has one price a day, the Net Asset Value, worked out after the market closes. Whether you order at 9 a.m. or 3 p.m., you get that same end-of-day price. An ETF’s price moves all day, like a stock’s. Buy at 10 a.m., and you might pay a different price than someone who buys the same ETF at 2 p.m.

How they’re managed. Many mutual funds are actively managed: a person or team picks what to buy and sell, trying to beat the market. Most ETFs are passive. They track an index, like the S&P 500 or the S&P/TSX Composite, with no one trying to outguess the market.
This isn’t a fixed rule. Active ETFs exist, and so do low-cost index mutual funds. But it’s the general pattern, and it’s a big part of why fees differ so much.

items.title: A MUTUAL FUND
items.text: Bought through a bank or adviser. Priced once a day, after the market closes. Usually actively managed. Typical MER around 1.5% to 2%.

items.title: AN ETF
items.text: Bought through a brokerage, like a stock. Priced all day while the market is open. Usually passive. Typical MER 0.05% to 0.25%.

blocks.text: CREDIT PULSE SPOTLIGHT: USE A LIMIT ORDER, NOT A MARKET ORDER

All-day pricing cuts both ways. A mutual fund buyer never has to think about this, since every order fills at the same end-of-day price. An ETF buyer does. A market order fills right away at whatever price is on offer, which for a thinly traded ETF, or in a jumpy few minutes, can be worse than the price you just saw. A limit order fixes that. You set the highest price you’ll pay to buy, or the lowest you’ll take to sell, and the order only fills at that price or better. It might not fill instantly, but it protects you from a bad surprise. For a widely traded, broad-market ETF, this rarely matters much. For anything less traded, it’s a smart habit, and it costs nothing extra. Also check your brokerage’s trading fee. Many now charge $0 to buy ETFs.

items.title: “Active management means someone is protecting my money from market drops.”
items.text: Active managers try to beat the market, but decades of research show most fail to do it over time, especially after fees. Active management isn’t a safety net. It’s a bet that a manager can outguess the market, made at a higher cost.

blocks.text: CREDIT PULSE SPOTLIGHT: PASSIVE DOESN’T MEAN CARELESS

The word “passive” undersells what’s going on. A passive index ETF isn’t unmanaged. It is kept matched to its target index, without anyone making judgment calls about which stocks to favour. When a company grows, it makes up more of the index and more of the fund. When a company shrinks, the reverse happens. Nobody has to decide to buy or sell. This isn’t a weaker version of active management. It’s a different approach: instead of guessing which companies will do best, you own the whole market and let the market’s own math do the work. That’s a big part of why passive funds cost less. There’s no team of analysts to pay for picking stocks.
A newer category worth knowing: all-in-one ETFs. Instead of buying separate ETFs for Canadian, U.S. and international stocks and bonds, one fund holds a ready-made mix of all of them.

These funds come in different risk levels, some heavier in stocks and some heavier in bonds, and they rebalance on their own to keep that mix steady. If you want a broad spread without managing several funds, this is often the simplest place to start. Pick the risk level that matches the Risk Tolerance lesson, not the one with the best recent return.
They usually charge a little more than a single-index ETF, since they bundle several funds together, but still far less than a typical mutual fund.

items.title: “ETFs are too complicated for a beginner investor.”
items.text: A single all-in-one ETF can be simpler than a mutual fund portfolio. One purchase, automatic rebalancing, a broad spread and a low fee. There’s a good case that it’s the more beginner-friendly option.

sections.title: Choosing between a mutual fund and an ETF

items.title: I understand both hold similar investments. The difference is how they’re built, not what’s inside.
I know whether my current holdings are actively or passively managed.
I’ve compared the MER of what I hold against a comparable ETF option.
I understand ETF prices move throughout the day, while mutual fund prices are set once daily.
I’ve considered whether an all-in-one ETF could simplify a portfolio I’m currently managing across several separate funds.

blocks.text: Wei’s spreadsheet
paragraphs: Wei worked as a dental hygienist in Markham. Over fifteen years, she had picked up four mutual funds, each suggested by a different bank adviser as her life changed: one for Canadian stocks, one for U.S. stocks, one for bonds and a balanced fund “for good measure.” She had never looked at them side by side.

After a coworker mentioned overlap between funds, Wei got curious. One evening she built a simple spreadsheet: fund name, MER and the top ten holdings of each. The pattern surprised her. Three of the four funds owned many of the same big banks and tech companies, and each one charged its own fee to hold them.

Her total fees came to about 1.9% a year. She felt a flash of anger, then a stronger urge to fix it all by Friday. She could sell everything at once, or she could get a second opinion first. She booked an hour with a fee-only planner, someone paid by her, not by the funds.

The planner checked two things before anything moved. All four funds sat inside her RRSP and TFSA, so switching wouldn’t trigger tax. And none of them charged a fee to sell. Then they matched her current mix of stocks and bonds to a single all-in-one ETF with an MER of 0.24%.
Over two weeks, Wei sold the four funds and bought the one ETF, using limit orders. Her yearly fees dropped from about $3,400 to about $430 on her $180,000 portfolio.
Wei kept the spreadsheet, though. It now has one row instead of four. She checks it every January, the same week she gets her own teeth cleaned.

blocks.text: Mutual funds and ETFs both pool money into broad baskets of investments. The real differences are how you buy them, how they’re priced and, usually, how they’re managed. ETFs trade like stocks all day, while mutual funds are priced once a day. Passive index funds track the market instead of trying to beat it, which is a big reason they tend to cost far less.
Look at what you own in one place, and you may find you’re paying twice.
blocks.detail: Lining up your funds side by side shows overlap and fees that separate statements hide.
blocks.extra: Section 08 helps you build your own fund list.

items.title: List every fund you hold, and note whether each one is a mutual fund or an ETF, and active or passive.
Check for overlap: are you paying several management fees to hold many of the same companies?
If you want to simplify, look into an all-in-one ETF at a risk level that fits your goals.

blocks.text: Worksheet: your fund inventory

Answer guidance: if you’re not sure whether a fund is active or passive, the fund facts sheet usually says near the top. It’s worth five minutes to check each one. If you find real overlap, talk it over with an adviser. You may be paying more than once for the same thing.

items.title: ETF
items.text: Exchange-Traded Fund. A fund that trades on a stock exchange all day, like a stock.

items.title: Net Asset Value (NAV)
items.text: The once-a-day price at which mutual fund units are bought and sold.

items.title: Active management
items.text: A fund manager picking what to buy and sell, trying to beat the market.

items.title: Passive management
items.text: A fund that tracks an index, with no manager picking individual investments.

items.title: All-in-one ETF
items.text: A single fund holding a ready-made mix across regions and types of investment, rebalanced on its own.
